articles.title: Jordanian security officer killed in stabbing attack in Amman
articles.author: Aseel Saleh
articles.content: One Jordanian police officer was killed and another was injured in a stabbing attack outside the Sri Lankan embassy in Jordan’s capital, Amman, on Thursday, November 5. According to a statement issued by Jordan’s Public Security Directorate (PSD), the slain officer was identified as Corporal Jawad al-Salaytah. PSD also confirmed that the perpetrator was arrested by a police patrol that rushed into the site of the attack. Jordanian Government Communication Minister and Official Government Spokesperson Mohammad Momani said that the preliminary investigation revealed that the assault was a “cowardly terrorist attack.” Momani affirmed that “attacking security personnel while performing their duty is an assault on the prestige of the state and the rule of law, and an assault on every Jordanian.” Local news outlets indicated that as per his judicial record, the attacker was previously convicted in 2020 in a terrorism case linked to the Islamic State of Iraq and Syria (ISIS), and sentenced to nine years in prison and temporary hard labor. The available information in the record further shows that he was released a few weeks ago after serving his sentence. The offensive against the police officer came three weeks after a shooting attack targeted a church in Jordan’s southern governorate of Karak, killing nine people. The Jordanian authorities announced at the time that the attackers were linked to terrorist groups in southern Syria, and retaliated by striking their positions in Rural Daraa. However, the airstrikes on Daraa left eight Syrian civilians dead – an incident for which Jordan expressed “deep regret” after the Syrian government summoned the Jordanian ambassador to Damascus in protest. An unnamed Jordanian source explained that the victims were killed by the pressure of the blast while sheltering in a tent near an ISIS hideout. Jordan has for decades been seen as a stable country despite its location between regional flashpoints such as Syria, Iraq, and the occupied West Bank. Yet, recent developments have raised concerns among many that these events could be part of a broader scheme to destabilize the country.

articles.title: South Korea moves to join Iran War under US pressure
articles.author: Ju-Hyun Park
articles.content: South Korea’s government has begun procedures to potentially join the US-Israeli war of aggression against Iran. On November 5, a vice-ministerial meeting affirmed a decision to expand the military capacities and operational area of the Cheonghae Unit, a blue-water naval force that has operated in the Gulf of Aden near the Red Sea as part of an “anti-piracy” mission since 2020. The revised mandate of the Cheonghae Unit would double its deployment area up to the waters of the Arabian Sea south of Duqm, Oman. This would place Republic of Korea (ROK) naval units on the fringes of the Gulf of Oman and the Strait of Hormuz – areas Iran has declared closed to foreign military vessels. The proposal would further expand the Cheonghae Unit to include P-8A Poseidon maritime patrol aircraft, an Explosive Ordnance Disposal (EOD) team, and unmanned mine-clearing equipment. An ROK defense ministry official told Yonhap News Agency that the expansion is being undertaken “to protect our citizens and safeguard our economic interests,” adding that the Cheonghae Unit’s new mandate would include support for “efforts to restore freedom of navigation in international shipping routes.” The official added that maritime patrol aircraft would be “prohibited from monitoring Iranian territory, territorial waters, or the interior of the Strait of Hormuz.” Per ROK law, the decision must now be approved by the Cabinet and President, followed by a vote in the National Assembly, South Korea’s parliament. The decision is expected to be made next week. War by deception Word of the ROK’s potential deployment to the Strait of Hormuz leaked in early September, following months of US pressure. Large protests attended by thousands swept the country, with the ROK’s major progressive forces presenting a united front against the war. On September 18, President Lee Jae Myung told media that his government had “ruled out” joining the war – but hinted that expanding the Cheonghae Unit’s deployment could be possible under the auspices of defending freedom of navigation. While it was widely reported internationally that Lee had ruled out support for the war on Iran, progressive parties and anti-war organizations in the ROK continued to raise the alarm. Many pointed out that expanding the Cheonghae Unit to the Gulf of Oman or the Strait of Hormuz would violate Iran’s prior warnings that foreign military vessels in these areas would be treated as enemy combatants. Given the circumstances, these organizations accused President Lee of misleading the public and attempting to proceed towards war by deceptive means. These warnings have proven to be prescient. The Lee administration’s claim to expand the Cheonghae Unit to protect freedom of navigation and commercial vessels is at odds with the details of the proposal. The new weaponry slated for addition to the Cheonghae Unit goes well beyond what would be required for a naval escort. As the Korean Confederation of Trade Unions, a progressive umbrella union organization representing over 1 million workers, put it: “If the true objective were merely to protect vessels, there would be no need for EOD teams, anti-submarine patrol aircraft, or mine-clearing equipment. These are military preparations unrelated to the protection of ships; they clearly reveal an intent to participate in an illegal war led by the United States.” While the Lee administration is maintaining that it would uphold independent command of its troops, the Cheonghae Unit in fact operates as part of the US Naval Forces Central Command’s Combined Maritime Forces. One way or another, the potential deployment shows every indication of either directly or indirectly supporting US military operations. The ROK Progressive Party, which holds four seats in the National Assembly, further pointed out that expanding Cheonghae Unit’s operational area amounts to a “deceptive, indirect deployment – a ploy to insert South Korea into the conflict,” adding that the waters from the Strait of Hormuz to the Gulf of Oman are “effectively a single theater of war…there is no buffer zone whatsoever between the two.” The Party statement also criticized the illegality of the potential decision. The Cheonghae Unit’s legal basis for deployment under international law, United Nations Security Council Resolution 1816, limits its operational mandate to Somalian waters. Furthermore, Article 5, Paragraph 1 of the ROK’s Constitution renounces wars of aggression. Under Washington’s pressure For months, South Korea staved off US pressure to join the war. In August, Trump suddenly announced the partial cancellation of Ulchi Freedom Shield, a major series of joint war drills held annually between the two governments. While citing his “very special relationship” with the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea (DPRK), Trump also delivered invectives against the ROK for its unwillingness to support aggression against Iran. Read more: ‘Unworthy of comment’: The DPRK rebuffs Trump’s overtures These demands have piled additional pressure on Seoul, which has also faced economic coercion under Trump’s tariff wars to deliver a massive $350 billion state-backed investment package into US industry. Lee’s domestic economic agenda is also being obstructed by the US military, and his government is in active dialogue with Washington to relocate the US Air Force Gwangju Base to make room for a proposed semiconductor manufacturing complex. The US and ROK are also negotiating the return of the latter’s operational control (OPCON) over its own military. Recently, US Forces Korea Commander Xavier Brunson declared that the conditions for the transfer had changed, and hinted that a return of OPCON before the end of Lee’s administration in 2030 would be unlikely. Given this context, it is likely that Lee’s proposed expansion of the Cheonghae Unit is an attempted maneuver to gain leverage in advancing his administration’s other goals vis-a-vis Washington. Lee would not be the first ROK leader to partake in US wars of aggression in the hope of advancing domestic pursuits. The ROK’s participation in the Vietnam War and the Second Gulf War were motivated by similar designs. However, Iran today is nothing like the Vietnam of the 1960s or the Iraq of the 2000s. Iran has demonstrated formidable military capabilities that have forced the US into a halting campaign which it can neither win militarily nor exit without facing severe loss of prestige. Regarding Seoul’s potential participation, Tehran has been clear: any foreign military operating in the Strait of Hormuz, the Gulf of Oman, or the Persian Gulf will be regarded as an enemy and its units and economic interests will be targeted. All this has compelled Lee’s government into contortions. Rather than straightforwardly backing the US war, Seoul is now engaged in a rather acrobatic performance that seeks to appease all sides. Technically, the ROK is meeting Washington’s demand, falling short of Tehran’s threshold for retaliation, and packaging it all in such a way that may avoid provoking a renewed wave of domestic outrage. Lee may believe this is the politically prudent thing to do. That illusion will rapidly fade if a single ROK casualty occurs.

articles.title: Paraguay’s right-wing president resigns as major bank collapses
articles.author: Pablo Meriguet
articles.content: Under the anguished, enraged gaze of millions of Paraguayans, the country’s right-wing president, Santiago Peña, announced his resignation amid opposition calls to initiate impeachment proceedings over his alleged responsibility for the closure of Ueno Bank, one of the South American nation’s most important financial institutions. “With the conviction that our republic must always take precedence over any individual or circumstance … I have decided to submit my resignation as president of the republic. I do so with the stability of our country, social peace, and the need to preserve our democratic institutions in mind,” Peña said in a televised address . Peña has been embroiled in serious allegations after his government transferred millions of dollars to Ueno Bank (nearly $850 million in public funds, including money from the Social Security system), an institution that announced its closure this week, despite having boasted for years of financial stability and growth in depositors, according to Manuel Gustale , former president of Ueno. However, on November 3, the Central Bank of Paraguay announced the bank’s dissolution after its solvency ratio fell below the minimum allowed under Paraguayan law. Hundreds upon hundreds of depositors at the bank in question took to the streets and demanded the return of their money, which was not possible due to the government’s freezing of the accounts. The situation is even more serious when one considers that a single business conglomerate managed to control not only the life savings of nearly all pension funds but also the savings of the majority of adults in Paraguay. Thus, the decision to freeze the accounts comes on top of several allegations of possible links between President Peña and the business group that controls Ueno Bank, which has raised suspicions of conflicts of interest involving Peña and Central Bank President Carlos Carvallo. For months, several Paraguayan institutions had been warning of a possible collapse of Ueno when it was discovered that the bank was granting excessive loans to companies linked to its own owners. “And yet, public funds kept flowing in. This isn’t simply the story of a poorly managed bank. It’s a system in which the bank, the regulatory body, and the presidency were so closely intertwined that none seemed capable of holding the others in check,” Orkun Saka, a professor at St. George’s University of London, told the BBC. Peña’s resigns after his party pursues impeachment But the final blow to the current administration came from its own party, the right-wing Colorado Party – which has governed the country for much of the past few decades – when former President Horacio Cartes (a member of the same party) announced that the party would support impeachment proceedings against Peña. “We will not stand idly by while public, private, and pension funds are plundered; we must think of the people and the values we uphold as the Colorado Party. We support the impeachment of the President of the Republic, Santiago Peña, in order to restore the Republic’s institutional framework,” Cartes said in a statement . Once Peña realized that his party (which was clearly aware of his past as a shareholder long before the crisis erupted) had withdrawn its support, he appeared before the cameras and announced that he would step down. However, the opposition and the Colorado Party stated that they would press ahead with the trial to determine the executive branch’s potential responsibility in the financial and political crisis rocking Paraguay. According to some reports , Peña was listed as a shareholder of Ueno Holding, a conglomerate of companies controlled to a greater or lesser extent by the Vázquez Group, the main shareholder group of Ueno Bank. And while Peña announced in early 2025 that he was no longer a shareholder of Ueno Holding, many question whether his political decisions regarding the institution were influenced by his own economic interests and those of the Vázquez Group. Added to this is the fact that the president of the Central Bank was also president of Ueno Bank, and that during Peña’s presidency, the Central Bank approved Ueno’s conversion into a bank in 2023. This highlights a close relationship between the executive branch and the failed bank. That is why opposition Senator Rafael Filizzola has said that the case constitutes: “the largest scam perpetrated by those in political power in the democratic era … It involves a bank created by those in political power to use public funds for private business ventures linked to political power, with the President of the Republic at the helm.” According to Filizzola himself, the losses from this case could amount to some $3 billion, which creates enormous uncertainty for the millions of Paraguayans who do not know when or if they will get their money back.

articles.title: Vegetation is claiming El Fasher, one year after it was depopulated by the RSF
articles.author: Pavan Kulkarni
articles.content: One year after the UAE-backed Rapid Support Forces (RSF) massacred tens of thousands of civilians in El Fasher, the capital of North Darfur state in war-torn Sudan, the city remains largely depopulated. Vegetation is claiming what used to be busy markets and roads. Hospitals are bombed out and empty, and the mass graves are quiet. This is the picture painted by the satellite imagery analysis by the Yale School of Public Health Humanitarian Research Lab (HRL) in a report titled “El-Fasher, One Year Later .”​ Human activity is largely limited to just five of the city’s 24,307 square kilometers, in the Daraja Oula neighborhood, where RSF troops are based. Except for the market in this neighborhood, none of the city’s other eight markets show signs of human activity. Six of them have been bombed, and two others subsequently fell into dilapidation. “At least five markets have vegetation overgrowth indicating an absent pattern of life,” stated the report, published on October 28, marking the anniversary of the fall of El Fasher, the last major city in Darfur region to hold out against the RSF. ​The RSF had captured the rest of this vast region, consisting of five states, soon after starting the war in April 2023 against its former partner in the military junta, the national army, called the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF). SAF’s only major base in this region was in El Fasher. Following a 20-month-long siege – starving the population with famine by cutting off food supplies – the RSF, which had been repeatedly bombing its hospitals and markets, finally launched a ground invasion on October 26.​ The SAF did not send reinforcements or air support. Many of its troops surrendered or fled. The local youth, organized as the Popular Resistance, took to the trenches and held out for nearly three days until the evening of October 28, when El Fasher’s Resistance Committee announced that “the last resisting soldier fired his last bullet” and “then fell as a martyr.” ​ Read more: El Fasher’s last stand: “The city has fallen, but its dignity has not” ​ RSF troops went on a killing spree, neighborhood to neighborhood, door to door, to depopulate the city. Daraja Oula, presently the only neighborhood with signs of human activity centered around the RSF, was the last civilian refuge in El Fasher. “Yale HRL identified burning activity consistent with human remains at 19 locations [in this neighborhood],” added the HRL report published on the first anniversary. ​ One of the locations is right outside the Al-Saudi Hospital. Attacking the hospital, the RSF “executed physicians, nurses, hospital staff, patients, and their families.” ​The bloodshed was so enormous that satellite photos showed reddish discoloration of the ground in many areas. Many of these red patches were strewn with “objects” measuring “approximately 1.3 – 2.0 meters, which is the expected range of a human body of average height lying horizontally,” HRL reported on October 28, 2025.​ As it continued to massacre civilians over the next days, satellite images as of November 1, 2025 showed at least 150 “clusters of objects consistent with human remains”, added a subsequent HRL update, which concluded that the “RSF has systematically killed and disposed of a number of objects consistent with human remains, likely in the tens of thousands.”​ Read more: RSF has burnt and buried tens of thousands of corpses in El Fasher, says Yale report ​ The report on October 28, 2026, the anniversary of the fall of El Fasher, reiterates this estimation, pointing out that 70,000 people are missing. They are neither visible in satellite images nor in the records of humanitarian organizations in Tawila, where survivors who managed to flee have taken refuge in IDP camps. A UN fact-finding mission concluded in February that RSF’s mass killings had the “hallmarks of genocide”. Now in November, the RSF continues the war in its fourth year, and the UAE continues to supply it with arms and vehicles, through Chad in Sudan’s west and Ethiopia in its east.​ Read more: The war in Sudan is “between two wings of a comprador parasitic capitalist class”

articles.title: 40 years later, calls grow demanding the truth about Samora Machel’s death
articles.author: Nicholas Mwangi
articles.content: Forty years after the death of Samora Machel, Mozambique’s first president and leader of the country’s liberation movement (FRELIMO), the circumstances surrounding the plane crash that claimed his life remain contested. The tragedy, which occurred on October 19, 1986, in Mbuzini, in what was then South Africa’s eastern Transvaal, continues to raise questions about whether the crash was an accident or an act of sabotage involving the apartheid government. At the 40th anniversary ceremony on October 19, 2026, Mozambican President Daniel Chapo said the investigations of the past four decades had not dispelled the doubts. Machel’s family joined the call, and a day later the government signaled that the case file may have to be reopened. His daughter, Josina Machel, expressed the family’s frustration. “If the investigation is open, then we need to know,” she told the gathering, asking investigators what information has been uncovered in 1986, 1996, and 2006, and whether anything new had emerged since. The family has made similar appeals at earlier anniversaries too. Mozambican president renews calls for clarity Mozambican President Daniel Chapo used the occasion to renew calls for the truth about the circumstances of Machel’s death, arguing that the investigations conducted over the decades had failed to eliminate the doubts surrounding the incident. He said the families of the victims and the peoples of Mozambique and South Africa had a right to know what happened on that October night in 1986. Chapo also connected Machel’s legacy to the continuing struggle for economic independence. He called for a Mozambique capable of producing more than it consumes, processing its own resources and creating employment opportunities, particularly for young people and women. “Samora’s generation won the freedom of the homeland. It is up to our generation to transform that freedom into prosperity for the people,” Chapo said. The Mbuzini plane crash On October 19, 1986, Machel was returning from Lusaka, Zambia, where he had attended a summit of African leaders. His presidential aircraft, a Soviet-made Tupolev Tu-134, went down in the Lebombo Mountains near Mbuzini, close to the borders of Mozambique and Swaziland, now Eswatini, in South African territory. The crash killed Machel and 34 other people, including members of his delegation and aircraft crew. Nine people survived. The location of the crash immediately raised questions. At the time , Mozambique was facing a devastating civil war, with the apartheid government of South Africa providing support to the RENAMO insurgency seeking to overthrow the FRELIMO government. Machel had also been a vocal supporter of liberation movements fighting white-minority rule across Southern Africa, including the African National Congress (ANC). The political relationship between Mozambique and Apartheid South Africa was therefore deeply hostile. Mozambique’s support for regional liberation movements had made it a target of South African destabilization efforts. The apartheid government regarded Machel’s government as a threat to its regional interests. Against this, suspicions emerged that the crash might not have been an accident. Competing investigations and unanswered questions Following the crash, a Commission of Inquiry headed by South African Judge Cecil Margo was established to investigate the circumstances. Its findings attributed the accident to pilot error, concluding that the flight crew had failed to follow the required procedures during an instrument approach and had continued descending without maintaining the minimum safe altitude. However, a Soviet investigative team disputed the findings. Its minority report argued that a false or decoy navigation beacon had misdirected the aircraft, causing it to turn away from its intended route and into the mountainous terrain near Mbuzini. The Soviet delegation also denounced that its expertise and experience had been undermined during the inquiry. It maintained that the aircraft’s unexpected 37-degree turn was central to understanding the crash and rejected the conclusion that pilot error alone explained the tragedy. The different findings left important questions unresolved. The matter was revisited by South Africa’s Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC) , established in 1996 to investigate human rights violations committed during apartheid. Its special investigation into Machel’s death examined the earlier inquiries, interviewed witnesses and considered evidence concerning the political and security circumstances surrounding the crash. The TRC did not establish conclusively whether the aircraft had been deliberately brought down. However, its report raised questions about the conclusions of the Margo Commission and highlighted evidence that warranted further investigation. Among the issues examined was the possibility of a false navigation beacon and the failure of South African authorities to warn the aircraft about the danger posed by its flight path. The report also considered testimony about a suspicious electronic device reportedly found near the crash site. A television journalist who attended the on-site investigations by the joint Soviet, Mozambican, and South African team told the Commission that an investigator had shown the television crew a device that could have been a frequency scrambler. While members of the Margo inquiry team reportedly told a journalist that the device had been found to be harmless, an expert on mobile beacons told the TRC that such a device could potentially interfere with an aircraft’s signal. The Commission’s final conclusion was that the investigations had raised questions that remained unanswered. It stated: “The investigations conducted by the Commission raised a number of questions, including the possibility of a false beacon and the absence of a warning from the South African authorities. The matter requires further investigation by an appropriate structure.” That recommendation has never been carried through. Nelson Mandela and Thabo Mbeki both promised to reopen the inquiry, and a police investigation, announced in 2012 after new documents surfaced, produced no public findings. Samora Machel’s revolutionary legacy Beyond the circumstances of his death, the 40th anniversary also brought renewed attention to Machel’s place in the history of African liberation. Born in 1933, Machel became involved in the struggle against Portuguese colonial rule and joined the Mozambique Liberation Front, FRELIMO, which was established in 1962. He rose through its military and political ranks, eventually becoming the movement’s leader following the death of Eduardo Mondlane in 1969. Under his leadership , FRELIMO intensified the armed struggle against Portuguese colonialism, which culminated in Mozambique’s independence on June 25, 1975. Machel became the country’s first president and led the newly independent state through a period of socialist-oriented transformation. His government pursued nationalization and expanded public provision in areas such as education and healthcare, while seeking to dismantle the economic and social structures inherited from colonial rule. It also supported liberation movements across Southern Africa, providing political and material solidarity to those fighting apartheid and white minority rule. This position placed Mozambique in direct confrontation with the apartheid government. South Africa supported RENAMO as part of its wider regional strategy to undermine governments and liberation movements opposed to apartheid. The resulting conflict devastated Mozambique, causing widespread displacement, destruction of infrastructure, and loss of life. Machel’s death therefore occurred within a wider regional struggle in which the survival of independent African governments and the liberation of Southern Africa remained closely connected. His political legacy continues to resonate across the continent, particularly through the principles of anti-colonialism, African solidarity, and self-determination. His famous revolutionary slogan, A luta continua (The struggle continues), remains associated with the liberation movements and generations of activists who challenged colonialism, apartheid and imperialism. The history of Africa’s liberation struggles is also marked by the assassination of other revolutionary figures, including Amílcar Cabral, Patrice Lumumba, Titina Silá, and Chris Hani, as well as the killing of Steve Biko under apartheid detention. While the circumstances of these deaths differ, they form part of a broader history in which political violence was used against leaders and movements challenging colonial and minority-rule systems. Machel’s death continues to be considered within this historical context, although the allegations surrounding the Mbuzini crash have never been conclusively established.

articles.title: How billionaires rigged the midterms (it wasn’t just Elon)
articles.author: Amanda Yee
articles.content: The 2026 midterms shattered records as the most expensive election in U.S. history, with an unprecedented $12 billion that flooded campaigns nationwide. BreakThrough News journalist Amanda Yee discusses how behind the massive price tag lay a coordinated ruling-class offensive: billionaire oligarchs and special interest PACs, from AIPAC targeting pro-Palestine progressives to Big Tech and crypto power brokers, bought bipartisan influence to deregulate industry, crush dissent, and protect corporate wealth. Yee explains who wrote the checks and reveals how America’s electoral system was engineered to serve capital over the working class. #breakthroughnews ****** Rough transcript follows: $12 billion—that’s how much was spent on the 2026 midterms, marking them as the most expensive elections in U.S. history. Here are the top contributors to this midterm cycle, according to OpenSecrets. If you look at the bar graph, it’s essentially a who’s who of billionaires. Elon Musk is at the top, followed by Zionist casino magnate Miriam Adelson and Michael Bloomberg. A bunch of tech oligarchs, including the LinkedIn co-founder and the CEO of Blackstone, are also on the list. Republicans have outraised and outspent Democrats across the board this cycle. However, the real story isn’t the party split; it’s who’s writing the checks and what they’re buying. Three special interest groups have dominated this cycle, spending historic amounts to shape Congress in their favor: AIPAC, big tech, and crypto. Let’s start with AIPAC. AIPAC contributed nearly $25 million to candidates and political committees in 2026 through September 30th. After September 30th, support for Israel became a massive political liability due to the ongoing situation in Gaza. More candidates are facing scrutiny for taking AIPAC money. In October, AIPAC announced they would no longer issue endorsements or make direct contributions to candidates. However, this doesn’t mean they’re stopping their spending; they’re just changing how they spend. This is where the United Democracy Project (UDP), AIPAC’s affiliated super PAC, comes in. UDP acts as a cover for AIPAC money. You might remember them from 2024 when they spent over $9 million to unseat Jamal Bowman and another $9 million to defeat Cori Bush. Both candidates were critical of Israel and lost their races after UDP’s involvement. AIPAC’s biggest investment in the primaries was a flop. In the Michigan Democratic primary, AIPAC and UDP spent $30 million trying to protect Haley Stevens’s seat, but she lost to Abdel Sayed. UDP then spent $9 million in the general election to support Republican Mike Rogers. AIPAC funds Democrats too, especially when they’re running against progressives. For example, in California’s 14th congressional district, AIPAC is backing Melissa Hernandez against progressive Democrat Aisha Wahab. Wahab, who has called the situation in Gaza a genocide, won a special election to finish Eric Swalwell’s term. UDP spent $1.6 million across both races to block Wahab, including $800,000 on attack ads. Individual billionaire donors also shape Israeli policy. Robert Kraft, a major donor to UDP and AIPAC, and Miriam Adelson, who donated over $66 million this cycle, are significant contributors. Hedge fund billionaire Paul Singer gave $49 million to Republican-aligned PACs and $2.6 million to UDP. Now, let’s talk about big tech. Elon Musk took the top spot for highest donor, contributing $446 million to Republican candidates and PACs. Over $200 million went to Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton’s Senate campaign. Musk also donated $5 million to Texas Governor Greg Abbott’s reelection bid. Other notable tech donors include Benjamin Horowitz and Mark Andreessen, who spent over $55 million and $43 million, respectively. OpenAI co-founder Greg Brockman and his wife Anna contributed $50 million to Republican causes. These donors launched the “Leading the Future” PAC to fund candidates committed to blocking AI regulation and cutting China out of the AI race. Finally, let’s discuss crypto. The Winklevoss twins, co-founders of Gemini Crypto Exchange, contributed nearly $24 million, mostly to MAGA Inc. Chris Larsen, founder of Ripple Labs, donated at least $22.5 million, with $12 million opposing California’s proposed billionaire wealth tax. Larsen also supports the “Invest in Tomorrow Coalition” PAC, which targets Republicans and DSA members who oppose renewable energy incentives. Fairshake, crypto’s own PAC, spent $95 million this cycle, backing 33 House incumbents. They’ve disclosed at least $1 million in donations to campaigns of key committee members like Brian Steil, French Hill, and Bill Huizenga. Fairshake also contributed to Democrats like Janelle Bynum, Derek Tran, and Steven Horsford. House Ways and Means Committee Chair Jason Smith, who has tried to subpoena Breakthrough over funding, is also backed by Fairshake. In conclusion, whether it’s foreign policy, AI regulation, or crypto protectionism, $12 billion bought significant access this election. This cycle encapsulates the rule of billionaires in the U.S., where choices are influenced by AIPAC, big tech, or crypto.

articles.title: The Country Says “No” to Trump: Not Just Congress, the Blue Tsunami Flips Statehouses Across U.S.
articles.content: We examine the results of Tuesday’s historic U.S. midterm elections with Daniel Nichanian, editor-in-chief of Bolts . In addition to taking back the House and Senate, Democrats also made major gains at the state level and will control a majority of governorships for the first time in 16 years. Democrats also flipped 12 state legislative chambers. “The size of the wins for Democrats in statewide races was wild,” says Nichanian. He identifies protecting abortion access, bolstering unions and ending police cooperation with ICE as some of the priorities Democrats are likely to pursue.

articles.title: First Gen Z Congresswoman: DSA’s Melat Kiros on Corruption, Medicare for All & Israel
articles.content: The Democratic Socialists of America made major gains in this year’s U.S. midterms, electing not just the largest-ever socialist bloc to Congress, but also winning dozens of races at the state, county and municipal levels. Democracy Now! spoke with Congressmember-elect Melat Kiros on election night following her victory in Denver, Colorado. She identified Medicare for All as her top priority and said progressives must lay the groundwork “so that in ’29, when we have the House, the Senate and the White House, we can sign it into law on day one.” Kiros is a 29-year-old Ethiopian immigrant and lawyer. In 2023, Kiros wrote an open letter about the danger of conflating antisemitism and criticism of Israel, for which she was fired by her law firm. She won a major upset in the Democratic primary earlier this year against longtime incumbent Congressmember Diana DeGette.

articles.title: “They Have Eyes”: How Trump’s Corruption Became a Top Concern for Midterm Voters
articles.content: Democrats regained control of both the House and the Senate in Tuesday’s historic midterm elections, a comeback fueled largely by voter anger over high prices and the war on Iran. But surveys also found that corruption was a major concern, with 76% of voters telling a Harris poll that elected officials care more about enriching themselves than improving the economy for ordinary people. A separate Reuters/Ipsos poll found that 63% of Americans considered it inappropriate for Trump and his family to profit from cryptocurrency, while 69% said his private business interests influence his decisions as president. “If this election was about corruption and cost, then this next Congress needs to be focused on accountability and affordability,” says Donald Sherman, the president and CEO of Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, or CREW . “Congress needs to do oversight not just on the administration’s corruption, not just on the president’s profiteering, but also on corporate America, what they have gotten out of engaging in the president’s pay-to-play environment, how corporate America and the outside influence of money in our political system has undermined the public voice in our policy discussions.”

articles.title: France’s student strikes
articles.author: Danielle Bullock
articles.content: F rench students have been protesting in the largest numbers since the historic May 1968 Paris uprising. Protests began last month in Paris’s northern suburbs, where students have struggled to learn in crumbling, pest-infested schools with too few teachers. Students say the government’s latest budget isn’t enough to fix the school system’s failings, and they are demanding more. Public anger over the budget and abysmal school conditions has spread—and so have the protests; students have been blocking high schools and protesting in the streets in the thousands. The government’s response has been heavy-handed and violent; there have been many recorded incidents of police brutality against young and vulnerable high school students. On Saturday, Oct 17th, 550,000 students, parents, educators, and trade unionists across the country flooded the streets to demand drastic, immediate improvements to the school system. Laurent (pseudonym) is a 35-year-old Information Technology teacher in a public school located in a city in Brittany, France. The students at his school are not currently on strike, but have held a few small rallies in solidarity with striking students across the country. I spoke with him to get his impressions as a public educator witnessing student protests from inside the country. Danielle Bullock: What is currently happening in your school? Are students on strike? Laurent: I work in a school near the city of Rennes, and there’s not a lot of protest here (in my school) for basically two reasons. One being that most of our students come from a sort of wealthier background, and they are not that involved in politics because they don’t have to be. So we just have a smaller number of students who are really involved in politics. And one other factor is most students come in with the bus. So when they arrive, it’s just two minutes before classes begin. So you can’t quite block your high school if you don’t arrive one hour before. So what we have, what the director of (my) school said is, it’s okay to protest in front of the building, but everyone who wants to come in has to be able to come in. So what we had the first few days (of the student strike) was one to two hundred students in front of the high school protesting. But my high school has 1,200 students. So mid-range in terms of size. Starting the second day, most of the students were still back in school because parents had to write a note saying their kid was on strike. They had to justify why the kids were not at school. And so we had one or two days with sort of a bigger protest in front of the high school, and ever since, almost nothing. The fact that students come to our school by bus is really a huge factor. In the nearby city (Rennes), there are a lot more protests at the high schools, and those schools are completely blocked. And there’s also quite a bit of vandalism. Because it’s a city where, historically, whenever there is a protest, there is a lot of stuff that is destroyed and vandalized. So with this high school movement, it sort of follows the same trends. DB: And the university students in Rennes, are they on strike in solidarity? L: We have two big universities in Rennes. Big for France —they’re not the same size as American universities. There’s one (university) for science and one more for literature and politics and everything. And the one that teaches literature and foreign languages is always on strike whenever there’s something. So this time as well, they blocked the university . I didn’t hear much about the scientific one, the scientific university. Also, because the campus is really large, it’s really hard to block anything. There are dozens of buildings, smaller buildings. So I didn’t hear much from them, but I know that at the literature one, the students went on strike as well. DB: What do you think is the main reason why the students are on strike? L: It’s quite difficult, actually, because it started as really a local thing because there are some high schools, especially near Paris, that are in really complete disrepair. And their first ask was: we want to be able to study in good conditions. For example, we want classrooms that aren’t 8 degrees Celsius (40º F) in the winter and 40 degrees Celsius (104º F) in the summer. We want teachers because when teachers are absent, or there are vacancies, there are no substitutes. We want chairs for everyone. We want tables for everyone, which is not quite the case in all of these (schools). Some high schools, especially near Paris, are in really complete disrepair. And [the student strikers’] first ask was: we want to be able to study in good conditions. But it’s quite a small number of high schools that have these sorts of issues. And these demands, I’ve been hearing about them for years now. And so the students started to do a bit of protesting. This time it went directly to blocking the high school because, back in my days as a high school student, first it was a protest in the street, and then, if nothing happened, we blocked the high school. This time they went with blocking first. With social media, there have been some videos of bins burning in front of high schools. Also, one big factor was that the political answer [to the strikers’ actions] was to send the police, and heavily armored police, directly. This really escalated the protests from the start. There have also been some videos of police violence against (what are) basically kids, and this is over social media, so it’s really spread rather quickly, which inspired other students who saw the videos and said, okay, we want to be part of that as well, and began to protest. DB: And what are the consequences of students not going to school if they were on strike? L: Where I am, there are no consequences. I mean, since most students go to class, the main consequence is that they don’t attend, so they fall a bit behind. But as far as I know, in my high school, the director is really more into dialogue. So he will let them speak if they want to speak. And if they want to protest, they can, as long as they don’t destroy anything. So where I am, the strategy is really not escalation at all. It’s just, okay, you want to protest? We will give you a place where to protest. They’re in dialogue with the director to talk about any issues, but the thing is, most of the demands are at a country level. So the director, he can’t do anything about these demands. When there’s no dialogue, of course, tension is building. And at some point, it has to burst. DB: Why did it have to come to this point where people are so angry? Students are so angry. L: The thing is that the students from the first high schools near Paris, they said we have been asking nicely for years, and we’re only heard when we start burning stuff. The current president has been ignoring what people in the streets have to say from the beginning. He’s never tried to discuss what people depend on. And even François Hollande before him, whenever there was a huge protest, he would send the police and just try to intimidate as much as possible. So basically, there is no dialogue between what people ask for and the government, and it’s been the case for ten to fifteen years now. That’s basically why everything’s coming to this point, because when there’s no dialogue, of course, tension is building. And at some point, it has to burst. DB: What is the general opinion of teachers about what’s going on with the strikes? L: I’ve been talking with colleagues. I mean, teachers, as everyone, have different political opinions. And people who are more on the right, to the far-right side, they support the police and (they think) all these kids should go back to school. [They say] they’re ridiculous, their demands are childish, and they should go back home or go back to school. From a more left point of view, I mean, of course, we support what they ask for. Because basically what they want is better conditions to work in. So the demands are not quite localized [some demands are more generalized and appeal to wider layers]. For example, there are also huge school days, 8 a.m. to 6 p.m., with big gaps in the middle, so really exhausting for students. Some of them have a one-hour drive to go to school and the same to go back home, and they are completely exhausted. Another thing is, after high school, there is a system, a platform (Parcoursup) , where you register if you want to go on to higher education. And since the supply for higher education in France is not enough to meet the demand, there’s a lot of frustration about that system and that platform. And we can understand that this platform creates a lot of stress because it looks at old school reports for the entire high school [career]. So every bad grade, even two or three years before the end of high school, can mean that you have a worse report and mean that you cannot really get into the school [college] you want. So it’s a lot of pressure for a long time for the students, and that we can empathize with. So we support the demands. Then there are basically two categories of teachers. Some who say, we’re in France, and in France, if you want to get something, you really never get anything unless you break stuff first. So we’re really, yeah, there’s some vandalism, but that’s France; that’s how it is. And some others who are like, yeah, we support the demands, but it would be really better if there weren’t that much vandalism. So basically, you have the two opinions from what I’ve been seeing around me, my colleagues. DB: Have any of the teachers’ unions made statements in support of student strikes? L: You have unions that are more on the right side and many of them that are more on the left side, but there’s the one big one and a lot of smaller ones, which are still quite big. And we have the choice every couple of years. There are some elections to see which are the bigger unions and how they should be taken into account with the secretary of education. [This determines which union] will have a bigger voice speaking with the secretary of education. So in France, teachers can go on strike if a union calls for it. And almost instantaneously, they all said, okay, starting now, you can go on strike. We cover you. DB: So—teachers can go on strike as well as students? L: Yeah, yeah, yeah. DB: When you say the union will “cover you”, what do you mean? L: They [the union] have to say, “We declare that there is a strike starting now. So that if we don’t go to work, it will be considered as participating in that strike instead of just, oh, I decided I don’t want to go to work. DB: Right, but teachers—there will be no other consequences for teachers? L: Right, so you won’t get paid, but you won’t lose your job, or you won’t have any kind of penalty. That’s how strikes work in France. You need the union that will say, ” Okay, as a union, we decided to go on strike.” And then every worker is included in that; we don’t have to provide proof that we are part of that union. We can just participate in that strike. DB: What are the teachers’ main complaints? If teachers had to say what the worst thing about French schools is, what do you think they would say? L: Oh, there’s a lot. Because the first strike for us this year was a week before the student strike started. Because basically, the prime minister announced his plan for next year’s budget. And in that budget, it was said that the pay would remain exactly the same. So basically, it means that we lose money because of inflation. And it’s been the case for basically years now. It started in the 80s. This difference between what we’re actually paid and inflation doesn’t follow exactly. And it means 20 to 30 percent pay cuts compared to what it was in the 80s. So it’s quite huge. That’s basically one major grievance—that teachers in France are quite underpaid. And so much so that there are a lot of problems recruiting new teachers. DB: In comparison to how much they pay police, do teachers make more or less? L: Yeah. The thing is, there’s one major difference that will make comparison quite hard—the level of qualification is really not the same. So if you were a teacher in France until recently, you needed five years of education, a master’s degree. And to become a police officer, you just need to have finished high school. So the bar is really lower. I would say police officers get slightly higher pay. I don’t know quite all the details, but at least in the beginning, their pay is better. DB: So less qualifications, better pay. L: There’s probably way more teachers than there are police officers in France, because almost everything is public. I think there are 800,000 teachers in France. So it’s quite huge. So if you want to raise their pay, it’s billions [of dollars]. Even if the increase isn’t really high, it’s billions instantly. It’s in this context that the state doesn’t have much money; it’s quite hard [for the state] to increase our pay. And the unions, they say, we will not negotiate a pay increase without also negotiating working conditions. Because what we had a couple of years ago, our secretary said, ” Yeah, so we will give you a pay increase.” But what he did basically was create another way for us to do extra hours, which would then get paid, which is not quite the same as, okay, you’re getting a pay increase. No, it’s an increase in labor too. And then a lot of things go with that. Since the pay is not quite good, we have trouble recruiting. So in many places, there aren’t enough teachers. So basically, in these places, in the places where people don’t want to go, there aren’t many teachers. And there aren’t many substitute teachers who are real [credentialed] teachers. There were some posts on eBay, yeah, we need a teacher. You need 15 minutes in front of someone who will say, ” Okay, you’re good. You can go in front of students,” and that is the whole process. That’s how the substitute teachers are recruited in some places. So the quality is really, it can be good because some of them can be good, but there’s no guarantee that the people who are in front of the students are any good at all. But many substitute teachers aren’t being hired right now. They’re not putting them in a classroom. DB: So what happens to a class when there’s no teacher? L: If the teacher gets sick, the class is canceled. There are two things. If the teacher is away for less than two weeks, they won’t even search for a replacement because it’s too difficult. If the teacher is away long enough and substitute teachers are available, you can ask for one. DB: So if somebody just gets sick, you get the flu, and you are out for five days, there’s no class. So what do students do when there’s no class? L: Yeah, usually in high school, they have some rooms where they can sort of relax and/or work if they want to. But if the high school is in a really bad state, maybe those rooms are quite horrible, or they don’t exist. So the inequalities are there as well. And no work for the students is provided. DB: How many students do you have at the most in a class? L: Classes go up to 35, 36, and that’s one of the reasons why I have a lot of students. The demand is that, okay, when we are having a full class all together, 35, 36 is way too many for one teacher to teach properly, so we want smaller groups. Because the state says teachers cost too much and cut the number of teachers, this led to bigger classes, even though the number of kids was rising at the time. Now we have the opportunity [to correct this] because people are having fewer kids, and the number of students in middle school and high school is slowly decreasing. And so basically there are two options. Either you keep the number of teachers the same, and you have smaller classes, or you decrease the number of teachers to follow the decrease in students. And there’s a big issue about how much we want to spend on education in France. That’s basically the one thing: what place we want to give education in our spending. And the politics that have been in France for many years is—we try to not invest much in public stuff. And yeah, probably private will develop. Oh, we’ll see. And that’s [true] for teaching, that’s [true] for health, that’s for most of the justice as well; it’s been underfunded for years now. All the public sector, except maybe police because there’s always money for police, and the army. But other than that, all the public sector, it’s been quite underfunded for years now. But that’s a choice that we have to make as a society. DB: How do you think the student strikes will be resolved? L: Unfortunately, after the riots last Saturday, I don’t have much hope for a happy ending. The videos of vandalism are everywhere to be seen, and they completely eclipsed the legitimate claims from the students. In the news, it feels like it sparked a bigger movement, and we’ll see if the students can keep their own strikes without huge interference from anyone else. In case of interference, the political right asks for a lot more police repression (against protesters). articles.title: Socialists and AI: No other choice?
articles.author: Chenglin Lee
articles.content: Thus [the bourgeois economist] saves himself from all further puzzling of the brain, and what is more, implicitly declares his opponent to be stupid enough to contend against, not the capitalistic employment of machinery, but machinery itself. —Karl Marx A s Marxists, we cannot disentangle Artificial Intelligence (AI) from capitalist political economy. AI is not, in fact, “intelligence” but rather a system of sophisticated algorithms that do not generate new ideas but can only spit out what it has been fed. How tech companies developed these algorithms was through “data scraping,” taking large amounts of personal and private data to teach its machines . AI is also not “artificial.” AI is powered and built by a large force of workers from the Global South, including Kenya, Venezuela, the Philippines, and India, among others. Moderators for digital platforms work 18 to 20 hours a day sometimes, at a rate of $1.46-$3.74 per day, looking at incredibly violent and disturbing text passages and images with no breaks . Of course, these digital companies offer no support to these workers, with many workers suffering from post-traumatic stress disorder and deep psychological damage. Many attempts to organize workers at these digital sweatshops have been crushed. Daniel Montag , a worker in Kenya, told Time that workers at a digital sweatshop subcontracted by Meta were all fired after attempts at unionization . Reading these reports is eerily reminiscent of the piecemeal sweatshops that Karl Marx described in Capital : worked to the bone under confined conditions for pennies. Digital infrastructure is not immaterial: the virtuality of the digital merely mystifies the grueling labor and extraction that enriches tech companies. This is coupled with the intensive fossil fuel and water use that AI data centers require, with AI data center needs exceeding the already heavy burden of other digital services such as Netflix and Zoom . Digital infrastructure is not immaterial: the virtuality of the digital merely mystifies the grueling labor and extraction that enriches tech companies. However, the moral arguments used to reject generative AI unfortunately often fall flat in the imperial core. Many ask, “Which major industry isn’t fueled by the blood of workers in the Global South?” Or, “Is it possible to be morally pure in a capitalist economy?” Of course not. But, if such arguments are not compelling, I offer here a few different arguments about why organizers on the Left should reject AI as it is being developed under capitalism. Community Writing, artistic expression, learning, and thinking are social acts. When we write or create art, we do so with the goal of reaching an audience intellectually or emotionally. When we read and think, we learn from writers and process what society, past and present, has communicated. As I often teach in my own writing courses, a key aspect to becoming a good writer is awareness of your audience and taking the opinions of others into account. For organizers, the social aspect is particularly important. As historical materialists, our writing and thinking should be continually developing with and in community. Generative AI takes away this community aspect, and the only interlocutor is the faceless user interface of Claude or ChatGPT. What potential organizing opportunities do we miss when we outsource community dialogue to machines? And why would we want to outsource idea-generation to machines that aggregate reactionary views? As studies have shown, AI algorithms commonly make decisions based on racial stereotypes . We should not risk reproducing these same reactionary tendencies in our own organizing by trusting machines that are often designed for surveillance and military applications. Also, nothing in the past five years has suggested that those in charge of these large AI companies, such as Mark Zuckerberg and Elon Musk, are interested in fixing the racist and reactionary tendencies of these systems. When organizers use AI, whether for writing or graphic design or anything else, we are feeding tech companies that actively seek to thwart our aims. The social effects of AI are horrifying: AI psychosis, cognitive decline, heightened surveillance, and militarization. When the U.S. military horrifically bombed a girls school in Iran, strong evidence suggests the target was chosen by an AI algorithm . When organizers use AI, whether for writing or graphic design or anything else, we are feeding tech companies that actively seek to thwart our aims. Feeding these tech companies our data also gives the surveillance state more ammunition to use against us. Our thoughts and ideas should be ours, not shaped by AI or given to tech companies as another data point to further suppress and surveil socialist organizing. Also, AI art is sloppy and ugly, and AI writing tends to be poorly written and formulaic. When restaurants use AI art, does the food not look like it’s infested with worms? Relying on AI hurts our ethos as organizers. Earlier this year, Vijay Prashad and Tings Chak were caught using AI to write an article on China and Uyghurs . The deeply problematic politics of their argument aside, the AI article contained several hallucinated sources that detracted from whatever credibility the article and the publication, Monthly Review , had. If our goal is to reach the wider community, we should not give the public easy grounds to dismiss us. And if we believe in the power of labor and creativity, our materials should reflect that. We can learn how to write and draw together, or at the very least pay competent writers and artists for our materials. This belief in community and labor should be centered in our thinking on AI, which leads me to the threat of AI and automation to labor. Labor Taste is ultimately subjective, and some people do genuinely love AI slop when it generates fingerless hands or worm-infested hamburgers. So, when discussing AI with the broader public, our arguments should center on labor. The dream of tech companies is to depress the value of labor power, so the capitalist class can extract more surplus value. We are beginning to see AI used in multiple industries: automated grading and teaching to replace educators, digitally generated art and content to replace artists, and vibes coding to replace software developers and engineers. The proliferation and development of AI poses a grave threat to workers. AI automation is not only targeting jobs of the professional managerial class either. Many companies are building AI-enabled robots to begin replacing jobs in factories and oil refineries. Even gig work is under attack by automation through companies such as Waymo and Starship Technologies. The proliferation and development of AI poses a grave threat to workers. According to one tracking tool , roughly 265,000 jobs have already been cut due to AI. The specter of AI is used in the way Marx describes automation in Capital, Volume I : The instrument of labour, when it takes the form of a machine, immediately becomes a competitor of the workman himself. The self-expansion of capital by means of machinery is thenceforward directly proportional to the number of the workpeople, whose means of livelihood have been destroyed by that machinery. The whole system of capitalist production is based on the fact that the workman sells his labour-power as a commodity. Division of labour specialises this labour-power, by reducing it to skill in handling a particular tool. So soon as the handling of this tool becomes the work of a machine, then, with the use-value, the exchange-value too, of the workman’s labour-power vanishes; the workman becomes unsaleable, like paper money thrown out of currency by legal enactment. That portion of the working-class, thus by machinery rendered superfluous, i.e., no longer immediately necessary for the self-expansion of capital, either goes to the wall in the unequal contest of the old handicrafts and manufactures with machinery, or else floods all the more easily accessible branches of industry, swamps the labour-market, and sinks the price of labour-power below its value. In other words, machinery and automation takes away the labor power of the worker, and the only commodity she has—labor—is rendered unnecessary. Workers who are not laid off now must work more as their workday intensifies to compete against machines. Machinery and automation takes away the labor power of the worker, and the only commodity she has—labor—is rendered unnecessary. Take, for example, an educator. A university begins to lay off instructors as tasks such as grading and curriculum development become automated by AI, and the remaining instructors take on more classes, more students, and ultimately more work to maintain their employment. The quality of education and instruction will decrease across the board for both students and instructors, but the university only sees short term value gains. In a capitalist political economy, where the goal is to extract as much value as possible, technology will always trend (with notable exceptions) toward automation, deskilling, and the suppression of the value of labor power. Spoiler alert for Park Chan Wook’s No Other Choice In Park Chan Wook’s newest film, No Other Choice , the main character, Yoo Man Su (Lee Byung Hun), is laid off from his manufacturing job at a paper factory. A new position at a paper factory opens up, and Man Su decides to eliminate his competition, literally. He kills every other unemployed worker competing for his position, and when Man Su gets the job at the end of the film, he walks into a factory where he is the only person. All other workers have been eliminated, and the only thing for Man Su to do is watch machines make paper. No community, no solidarity. Barely even any work. Park Chan Wook’s vision of automation grows ever closer as tech companies, large corporations, and governments promote and fund AI in service of value extraction, war, and surveillance. AI is another weapon aimed directly at the global working class, whose precarious conditions of daily living are already close to unbearable. Is the time we save outsourcing our creativity and cognition to automated algorithms worth it? articles.title: On election day, Trump announced the end of $4 billion aid to Israel by 2027
articles.author: Aseel Saleh
articles.content: US President Donald Trump told FOX News on Tuesday, November 3, that the US will stop providing Israel with the annual $4 billion in aid by the end of the year. Trump claimed that Israel does not need US assistance anymore to buy weapons, as it can do it on its own. “We were giving them $4 billion – we are – but it gets cut off at the end of the year,” Trump noted, claiming that the suggestion was brought forward by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. “Israel’s our number one. We give them more than anybody else, and they no longer need it.” The US president added. As per the existing security agreement that runs through 2028, the US provides Israel with roughly $3.8 billion in annual military assistance. Critics considered Trump’s announcement to be a desperate campaign move and electoral propaganda to influence voters as polls opened nationwide, by reassuring constituencies skeptical of mounting US foreign spending on the multi-front war across West Asia. Netanyahu had already expressed the intention to eventually end Israel’s dependence on US defense funding a few days before the Israeli election on October 27, justifying his position by saying the US “has changed.” Read more: Israel’s elections: all roads lead to genocide “If you think we’re going to continue receiving what I secured twice, and that’s tens of billions of dollars in American aid for the defense budget, prepare yourselves and get used to the fact that it won’t happen, because America has changed,” he declared. Many believe Netanyahu was referring to the growing opposition in the US against funding the Israeli war machine, in the aftermath of Israel’s genocidal aggression on Gaza and the atrocities perpetrated against Palestinians in general in the occupied territories. Read more: Three years of genocide in Gaza, the Palestinian people remain steadfast

articles.title: Violence is driving healthcare in northern Ethiopia to collapse, warns WHO chief​
articles.author: Pavan Kulkarni
articles.content: “The violence in northern Ethiopia is pushing an already fragile health system closer to collapse,” World Health Organization (WHO) Director-General Tedros Ghebreyesus warned on November 2, as civilian casualties mount from drone strikes in Tigray and Amhara.​ Earlier on October 30, a drone strike by the Ethiopian army killed at least 12 civilians and wounded many more in the town of Rama in the northern region of Tigray, where its troops are fighting the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF).​ The victims were gathering sorghum scattered across the road from a truck that was hit by another drone strike the previous night.​ In Tigray’s southern neighbor Amhara, where the federal government led by PM Abiy Ahmed is fighting the Amhara Fano National Movement (AFNM), drones struck the Hayiq Jari 2 Turk IDP camp five times in 15 minutes, killing at least 16 and injuring 22.​ While there was no fighting in and around the camp itself, Reuters reported that the AFNM had been nearby. The drone strike killed three pregnant women, a child, and several students on their way back from school were among the killed, Addis Standard reported . Adding that a newborn was also killed, Tedros called these attacks “deeply disturbing”.​ “While these are the latest incidents, drone attacks and civilian casualties have tragically become frequent across Ethiopia.”​ Earlier in September, several armed groups – many of whom were often pitted against one another by Abiy’s government – united to form the Alliance for Survival to overthrow his regime.​ Read more: Ethiopia plunges into civil war again as PM Abiy’s ‘divide and rule’ backfires ​ Drone strikes in October have killed scores of civilians and injured many more. Treating casualties is a major challenge. “Hospitals face shortages of health workers, medicines, and equipment. Ambulance services are severely limited. Insecurity is obstructing the delivery of life-saving medical supplies to some areas,” Tedors said, adding, “The best medicine is peace.”​
